title: Long-horizon work · Choosing an agent
description: Break extended work into resumable experiments with explicit state, gates and evidence. Match autonomy, cost and review effort to task risk, uncertainty and reversibility.

sections.title: A task grows beyond one sitting

blocks.body:
The retry helper now behaves as intended. A larger change follows: the team wants to replace its old configuration interface across several packages. Some callers use defaults, some pass explicit limits, and one service wraps the helper to translate errors.

An instruction to 'migrate all callers and remove the old interface' hides several decisions. We first need to understand which behaviours callers depend on. We then need a way to introduce the new interface without leaving the repository unusable halfway through. Finally, we need evidence that removing the old path will not strand a caller we missed.

A longer conversation does not settle those decisions. Neither does dividing the task into equal chunks of time. The useful stages follow the questions the work must answer.

The first stage can end with a caller map and a statement of the behaviour each group depends on. The next can introduce a compatibility path and show that existing callers still work. Another can migrate one representative caller and exercise it. Only after the remaining callers have been addressed does deleting the old interface become a well-supported next action.

This sequence is provisional. The wrapper may reveal an undocumented dependency on error identity. That discovery changes the plan: investigate and agree on the required behaviour before spreading the migration further. A stage is valuable partly because it creates a place for new evidence to change what happens next.

**Worked Example**

The agent has added the compatibility path and migrated one package. Its focused tests pass. It is late, and the process is about to stop. 'Migration progressing well; continue with the remaining packages' would leave tomorrow's session with most of the investigation still to reconstruct.

A useful handoff names the current revision and any uncommitted changes, points to the caller map, and records which package was migrated. It includes the exact checks that ran and the limitation: the service wrapper has not been exercised because its integration fixture is unavailable. The next proposed action is to inspect that wrapper before deleting any compatibility code.

Notice what this preserves. The next session knows a completed change, the evidence for it and an unresolved dependency. It can distinguish 'not yet migrated' from 'migrated but unverified'. It also knows why the apparently tidy next step of deleting the old path would be premature.

On restart, the session checks the workspace before following the note. Suppose a colleague has changed the wrapper in the meantime. The saved observation still describes the earlier revision, but it no longer establishes what the wrapper does now. Reinspect the affected part and update the plan. There is no need to throw away every result merely because one file changed; there is a need to identify which conclusions depended on it.

Chapter three introduced checkpoints as a way to preserve an investigation. Here the checkpoint also coordinates changes to artifacts. Keep the actual patch and relevant logs retrievable alongside the note. A summary saying 'package migrated' cannot restore a lost edit or prove which source a passing test exercised.

When work resumes, it should be able to explain its next action from that state. If it immediately repeats the completed caller survey, something useful was lost. If it refuses to revisit the changed wrapper, something tentative was made too permanent.

blocks.question: A checkpoint records a passing test, but the resumed workspace contains a later edit to the tested helper. What should the resumed run do?
blocks.answer: Inspect what changed and re-establish the relevant behaviour before relying on the old result. The recorded pass remains evidence about the earlier state. Preserve unrelated findings that still apply, while checking the conclusions affected by the edit.

sections.title: Recognise when more time is not helping

blocks.body:
A long run can spend its budget while staying in the same place. It retries a command, reformats nearby code, or writes a new plan without resolving the uncertainty that blocked the old one.

Ask what observation changed since the last stage. Finding a missing fixture is progress because it explains why a test cannot run. Obtaining that fixture enables a new experiment. Running the same command repeatedly without changing the setup usually adds little. Repetition may be justified for a flaky failure, but then it should be a deliberate experiment with a stopping condition and a record of outcomes.

Make the unfinished question visible. For the wrapper, it might be whether callers rely on receiving the first timeout object. If local evidence cannot establish that, the next useful action could be a question to the service owner. Giving the agent another hour without access to the necessary evidence will not answer it.

Budgets help contain such runs, but they should leave a useful stopping state. Record the findings, remaining changes and reason for stopping before the limit is reached where possible. An interrupted migration may contain a useful intermediate patch without being complete. Keep that distinction in the handoff.

Recovery also depends on the kind of action underway. Reading a file can usually be repeated. A request to publish a result may have succeeded even if its response was lost. Before repeating an uncertain external action, check its recorded identity and destination. The next chapter will develop this problem for unattended jobs.

sections.title: Grant autonomy to parts of the work

blocks.body:
For our migration, an agent can often survey callers, draft a patch and run local tests under an agreed scope. Changing a public interface or deploying the migrated service may require a separate decision. The workflow therefore has several degrees of autonomy within it.

Consider uncertainty, consequence and recovery together. A large local search can be inexpensive to redo. A one-line configuration change can redirect live traffic. Counting files or tool calls will not tell you which needs a closer decision.

Place review before a consequential transition and give the reviewer something specific to decide. 'Proceed?' beside an enormous transcript is a weak gate. 'The remaining callers use the new interface; these checks ran; the integration fixture is still unavailable; should removal wait for that check?' presents a decision and its evidence.

Do not require approval for every small read merely because a later action is consequential. Frequent low-value approvals consume attention and can encourage automatic acceptance. The aim is to give people a chance to settle questions that need their judgement while allowing the agreed work to proceed.

The enforcement must agree with this design. If publication requires approval, a credential available earlier in the run should not already permit the agent to publish through another path. The environment from chapter seven is what makes the intended division of responsibility real.

blocks.question: A migration can prepare and test a patch, but publishing requires review. When does that review lose its intended effect?
blocks.answer: When publication can already occur through the tools or credentials available before approval, or when approval happens after publication. A meaningful gate precedes the action and controls whether that action can execute.

sections.title: Let the trial change the scope

blocks.body:
A dependency upgrade offers a smaller place to practise this judgement. Let an agent inspect the proposed version, make a local change and produce the relevant test evidence. Keep the release decision with the existing owner while you learn what reviewing those outputs requires.

Several accepted patches may justify continuing that arrangement. They do not necessarily justify automatic releases: the trial has not exercised every release consequence. A useful expansion targets a particular remaining cost and comes with evidence about it. Creating a review branch automatically may remove routine handling without also granting permission to merge.

Measure failures and human effort as well as accepted outcomes. If the reviewer spends most of the time reconstructing what ran, improve the evidence handoff before expanding authority. If ambiguous upgrades regularly need product decisions, route those cases for discussion instead of treating every interruption as a defect in the agent.

Try the lab below with a task you know well enough to judge. Your conclusion may be to keep the present scope, reduce it, or permit one additional action. A narrow result can still save meaningful work.

We can now describe a task that progresses through stages and stops at intelligible boundaries. To make it recur unattended, something must select the right events, create the right environment and account for each outcome. That is where the next chapter begins.

data.title: Lab 5 · Choose an autonomy boundary
data.brief: Choose a real task that could span several sessions. Design a small trial that reveals where the agent can proceed and where another decision is needed.
steps: Identify intermediate results that would establish progress, and the uncertainty each stage should resolve.
Record the environment and actions permitted during the trial, including any separate publication decision.
Stop after a useful intermediate result. Resume from a checkpoint, then change one relevant fact and inspect how the continuation responds.
Compare the result and review effort with the current approach. Keep, narrow or expand one part of the scope, explaining what the evidence supports.
deliverables: A trial report with an expansion decision
data.review: Look for continuity of evidence and a meaningful decision at each review point. A short trial can reveal repeated work or a missing check; it cannot establish a rate of rare production failures. Keeping the current scope is a legitimate outcome.

heading: How can a long task keep making progress?
